catalog_quote: However, Eudeve and Huichol preserve clear evidence of this reconstructed PUA accentual contrast. In Eudeve, we cannot be sure what exactly was meant by the acute accent mark in the grammar and vocabulary now published by Pennington (1981). The anonymous 17th century Spanish author who wrote it could have been hearing stress or tone, but at least it seems likely that it was a prosodic feature of some kind. ... Crucially in both languages, in certain morphological classes, the acute accent appears to fall with almost perfect consistency on the syllable which I reconstruct as stressed in PUA. ... In Eudeve, we find the contrast only in one set of verb forms. Noun stems of both *CVCV and *CVCVC classes show accent on the second syllable in the nominative case and on the first syllable (the second syncopates) in the accusative and genitive, e.g., surá-t, súr-ta, súr-te 'seed' < PUA *sula ju…

sources.quote: p.100: 'of more importance are stress patterns, seen in Table 2. Toward the south, stress falls on the second syllable or a suffix. This occurs in Tr and Gu ... This usually occurs in Op, Eu and Tu. Stress is always initial in Ca. However, Op and Eu may have initial stress. Heath (1977) points out that stress in UA may have been variable with respect to verb morphology.' He lists 'development of initial stress' as a shared Op-Eu/Cahitan innovation. fn.2: 'an acute accent indicates stress'; interpretation of the Eudeve documents follows Lionnet (1979a) and Escalante (1964).
sources.locator: p.100 (section 'Vowels and Stress Patterns'); Table 2 'Stress Patterns' p.104; fn.2 (acute accent = stress in his transcription)
sources.note: Open comparative paper with an explicit Eudeve stress statement (usually second syllable/suffix, but initial stress also occurs) -- independent support that accent is not positionally fixed; downloaded and read now.

sources.note: The standard modern grammatical analysis (phonology, three noun declensions, verb paradigms + lexicon) of the same 17th-c. Arte; the record's secondary rule (accent shift + syncope arí-t/ár-ta, mecá-t/mé-ta) currently rests on es.wikipedia paraphrasing this book, and the record carries a 'Wikipedia only' caution. Its section on acento would state directly whether accent placement is lexical/morphological and settle the domain field.
